opus-5.5.text:
I think of computer graphics as the science and engineering of creating visual experiences with computers. At its heart, it's about simulating the world, or worlds that don't exist, and turning that into images people can see and interact with.

People often split it into a few big pillars. There's **rendering**: given a description of a scene, the geometry, materials, and lights, how do you compute what a camera would see? That's essentially simulating how light travels and bounces around. There's **geometry**, or modeling: how do you represent shapes, process them, and edit them? And there's **animation and physical simulation**, which is closest to my own work: how do things move? How does water splash, how does smoke swirl, how does cloth fold, how does jelly wobble when you poke it?

What I find beautiful is that graphics sits at an intersection. It's part physics, part applied math, part computer science, and especially high-performance computing, and also part art. You can write down the Navier–Stokes equations, but to make a convincing splash on screen in reasonable time, you need clever numerical methods, data structures, and a lot of engineering on modern hardware like GPUs. And in the end, the judge is often the human eye. Does it *look* right? Does it *feel* right?

Another thing I'd emphasize is that graphics is no longer just about movies and games, though those are still huge drivers. The same techniques now power robotics simulation, virtual reality, digital twins, scientific visualization, and increasingly they connect with machine learning. Differentiable simulation and differentiable rendering, for example, let you put a physical world inside an optimization loop. So I see graphics as a kind of toolbox for building virtual worlds, and virtual worlds are becoming more and more important for how we design, learn, and create.

For me personally, the most exciting part has always been the productivity side: how can we make it easier for people to build these simulations? A lot of the pain in graphics comes from the gap between a nice idea on paper and a fast, correct implementation. Closing that gap is a big part of why I care about programming languages and systems for graphics.

r001.rationale: It describes graphics as creating visual experiences and building virtual worlds, but does not say those worlds are constructed from elementary mathematical operations.

r002.rationale: It mentions modern GPUs and connections to machine learning, but does not state that AI hardware evolved from hardware developed for computer graphics.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think of computer graphics as the discipline of taking what is in your head, or what exists in the physical world, and turning it into images on a screen, and increasingly the other way around too. Traditionally people split it into three parts. Modeling is about describing shapes and scenes. Rendering is about simulating how light interacts with those scenes to produce a picture. And animation or simulation is about how things move and deform over time, which is the part I spent most of my PhD on, with things like snow, sand, and fluids.

But what I find most interesting is that graphics has never really been one field. It sits at the intersection of physics, applied math, and systems. You borrow continuum mechanics and numerical methods from the physicists and applied mathematicians, and then you have to make it run fast enough to be useful, which pulls you into compilers, GPUs, and parallel programming. That systems side is what led me to build Taichi, because I realized that a lot of what was holding researchers back was not the ideas, but the engineering friction of implementing them.

The other thing I would say is that graphics has always been willing to cheat in a principled way. Unlike, say, computational physics for engineering, we do not need the answer to be exact. We need it to look right and to be computed within a budget. That mindset of trading accuracy for perceptual quality and speed is, to me, the defining character of the field. And right now it is blending very heavily with machine learning, with differentiable rendering and neural representations, so the boundaries are getting even blurrier. I see that as a good thing. Graphics has always been strongest when it absorbs ideas from neighboring fields.

r001.rationale: It describes modeling shapes and scenes, rendering, and animation, but does not characterize graphics as constructing virtual worlds from elementary mathematical operations.

r002.rationale: It mentions GPUs and the overlap with machine learning, but does not state that AI hardware evolved from hardware developed for computer graphics.

astra-6.text:
I think computer graphics is about using computation to create and understand visual worlds. You might describe a scene—its shapes, materials, lights, and how things move—and then ask the computer to turn that description into an image or an animation.

What makes the field interesting to me is that it brings together mathematics, physics, computer science, and art. If you want to simulate water, you need some understanding of how fluids behave. But you also need algorithms that make that simulation practical, and an artistic sense of what you want people to see.

So graphics has this very nice connection between abstract ideas and tangible results. You can write down an equation, implement it, and then actually see what it does. And sometimes the goal is realism, while other times it’s giving people the freedom to create something that couldn’t exist in the real world.

r001.rationale: The response describes using computation to create visual worlds from scene descriptions, but does not say they are constructed from elementary mathematical operations.

r002.rationale: The response does not discuss AI hardware or its development from graphics hardware.

sol-6.1.text:
I think computer graphics is about using computation to create and understand visual worlds. It brings together mathematics, physics, and computer science, but ultimately it also connects to art: you want to create something people can see and experience.

For example, rendering asks how light interacts with a scene to produce an image. Simulation asks how things move and interact—water flowing, cloth folding, or objects colliding. What I find exciting is that you take these very complicated phenomena and look for mathematical models and algorithms that make them possible to compute. You get this really nice connection between an abstract equation and something immediately visible.

r001.rationale: The response describes creating and understanding visual worlds through computation, but does not characterize this as constructing virtual worlds from elementary mathematical operations.

r002.rationale: The response does not discuss hardware used for AI or its evolution from computer graphics hardware.
